zoning.code: El Cerrito Municipal Code Title 19 (Zoning), §19.06.030 Development Standards
zoning.tallPortionSetbacks: portions of building >25 ft tall require 10 ft side setback (and 20 ft rear when abutting an RS zone)

heightMeasurement.topReference: highest point of the structure (i.e. the roof ridge / top of covering) — NOT a midpoint; no sloped-roof averaging
heightMeasurement.gradeDatum: ground level directly below, at the lower of natural or finished grade (per part B); not an averaged datum
heightMeasurement.allParts: all parts of the building except listed projections must comply with the max height

notes: RM has NO daylight-plane requirement (unlike the RS districts); height is governed by the flat 35 ft cap.

Per §19.03.050, height is measured to the HIGHEST point of the roof from the ground directly below (lower of natural/finished grade) — no midpoint averaging, and the 2.5 ft crawlspace counts (it sits above grade=z=0).

DESIGN: raised plate (story-and-a-half), 2.5 ft attic perimeter wall -> eave at 25.0 ft AG (overhang fascia ~24.2 ft). Roof 8:12; structural ridge ~34.33 ft, top of covering ~34.96 ft — under the 35 ft cap but by only ~0.5 in. CAUTION: at 8:12 there is essentially no margin; confirm actual roof-assembly thickness or back off to ~7.75:12 for a safe ~3 in. The south shed dormer is a FLAT roof behind a 2 ft decorated parapet (coping + cornice + dentils), which stays well below the ridge.

Eave wall held AT 25 ft (not over), so the building walls do not trigger RM's >25 ft side/rear setback step; the roof + dormers rise above 25 ft, so confirm how the city applies the >25 ft rule to roof vs wall portions (ECMC §19.06.030 table).
8:12 yields ~820 sf >=5 ft and ~564 sf >=7 ft of attic floor (vs 643/439 for the eave-at-floor 10:12 scheme); the flat shed dormer gives a 7.5 ft clear ceiling over its bay.
Remaining to confirm: roof-assembly thickness keeps the ridge <35 ft; any RM story/floor-area cap; parcel designation 'RM5' shares the base RM standards in the §19.06.030 table.

lot._noteDepth: The parcel's N-S depth is DERIVED, not authored: the south line sits scullerySouthFt off the scullery and the north line is set by frontage.northYardFt, so the front yard holds whatever the house does. See lot_lines in builders.py.

deck._note: The rear deck. Its west and east edges are authored as CLEARANCES from the property lines — the same idiom as westMarginFt/scullerySouthFt — so the platform follows the parcel if widthFt or westMarginFt ever move. The south edge stays derived (scullerySouthFt plus the lot wall's 8 in) and the east terrace's north edge comes off the extension's north wall FACE, not its bounds: room bounds are wall CENTRELINES, so stopping at the bound would leave the wall corner 2.75 in proud of the deck.
deck._noteSteps: stepCount RISERS of base/stepCount (7.5 in over the 30 in crawlspace). A flight has stepCount-1 TREADS plus a flush grade paver, so it projects (stepCount-1)*treadFt past the deck edge — the existing inset flights emit stepCount slabs only because their top one is flush with the deck and fills a notch. Clear ground at the toe is therefore clearFt - (stepCount-1)*treadFt, not clearFt.
deck._noteEast: The east edge is NOT a clearance: the deck runs all the way to the SE corner, so it dies on the east CMU lot wall's inner face exactly as its south edge dies on the south wall's. Only the west edge is a setback. The NORTH edge of the east terrace is the existing deck's north edge — the family room's south wall — because running it further north brought the deck up the side of the house toward the front and cost the yard its privacy.

hotTub._note: Built into the deck. Its ENTRY SILL — the coping you step over — is FLUSH with the deck: recessRisers 0, so the decking runs right up to the stone band and there is no intermediate platform to step down onto first. The tub is still built in; what sits below deck level is the water, about 5 in down, which is what you step into. Dimensioned off the things it is actually measured from — the lot walls' INNER faces — rather than absolute plan coordinates, which this file authors nowhere else.

driveway._note: Two cars side by side on the east front yard. Anchored to the LEVEL stretch of the north frontage rather than to a coordinate: the public walk falls ~3 ft from the NW corner and dies to lot grade northLevelFromEastFt short of the NE corner, and the retaining wall stops at that same point. East of it is the one place a drive can cross the property line with no step and no gap cut in the wall, so the drive's WEST edge sits on that point and it runs east from there. Its south end is the yard fence — cars park against it.
driveway._noteWidth: widthFt must hold stallWidthFt twice over or it is not a two-car drive; ifc_check asserts exactly that rather than the 20 on its own, which is a number with no argument behind it.

yardFence._note: A 6 ft stained BOARD fence closing the rear yard: from the east extension's NE corner, east along that wing's north wall face, to the east property line. Its first 15 ft ride the new deck terrace.
yardFence._noteDatum: heightDatum says what the 6 ft is measured from. 'surface' = 6 ft above whatever it stands on, so it steps up over the deck and doubles as that edge's guard now the rails are gone. 'grade' = one flat top line 6 ft above grade, which over the deck is exactly 42 in — a code guard — and is the one-word retreat if a fence-height cap turns out to bite.

sidePorch._note: The side entrance: a small board porch at the east wing's outside door, filling the reentrant corner between that wing's north wall and the primary block's east wall. Dimensioned as a DEPTH only — its width is the wing's own ~11 ft and its south edge is the wing's north bound, so it follows the house rather than a coordinate. Deliberately plain: this is the door off the drive, not a second front stoop, so it gets a board deck where add_porch gets a stucco skirt and splayed cheek walls.
sidePorch._noteSteps: stepCount and treadFt are NOT authored here — the flight reads lot.deck's, so every set of steps on the lot climbs the same 7.5 in riser. stepWidthFt and the awning width are CENTRED ON THE DOOR and then snapped flush to the primary's east wall, which both land within a few inches of: a 3 in sliver of deck beside a stair reads as a mistake where a flush edge reads as built.

guard._note: The deck stands 30 in over the yard, so its two OPEN edges get a guard — the east edge and the north edge as far as the head of the stair. South and west are house walls, and the run's south end dies into the yard fence's terminal post, which already stands 3.5 ft above this deck; a second post 3 in from it would be a mistake, not a detail. (The rear terrace has no rails ON PURPOSE and this does not change that: there the whole open edge IS a flight of steps.)
guard._noteHandrail: The stair handrail's height is NOT authored. It is this same heightFt carried down the rake above the nosing line, which lands at 36 in — inside the 34-38 in a handrail is allowed — and makes the guard's top rail and the handrail one continuous line broken only at the newel. balusterOcFt is a MAXIMUM that each run divides evenly, not a pitch, so the 4 in sphere rule holds whatever length a run works out to. It is spacing in PLAN on the rake as well as on the level runs: the balusters are vertical whatever the rail above them does, so the opening is measured horizontally.

awning._note: A FREE-STANDING projection over the door — it stands clear of the porch on its own brackets, with nothing landing on the deck. springFt is the top of it AT THE WALL, above the porch floor, and it falls dropFt over its projection; the underside of the outer edge is what has to stay above head height, so that is what ifc_check measures rather than the mounting height.
awning._noteWidth: widthFt is a FALLBACK. The awning fills the wall's WEST BAY — the door's own room — which lands it exactly centred on the door with no snapping, and stops it dead on the party wall instead of straddling it. Authored at 6.0 ft it overhung that line by 6 in and drove through the elevation trellis's stile: a collision neither builder could see alone, since each measured from a different end of the same wall.

wingElevation._note:
The east wing's NORTH face: 10.9 ft wide by 19 ft of it, and the one wall on the house that takes no windows — the east bay is the bathroom on BOTH storeys, and its window is on the east face. Read as TWO STOREYS, which is how the house itself is built: a band of T1-11 on a belt course above, plain stucco below carrying only the door and its awning, and a raking entablature at the top. It began as four quadrants over the two REAL bays the rooms behind it make — the wall's centreline is the bath/vestibule party wall and the door sits dead centre of the west bay, which is why the door sits where it does — but the full-height trellis that held the east bay is gone, so the bays no longer divide the elevation and the belt course does.

Two things were tried here first and are worth not repeating: a blind oculus, which read as a porthole stuck on a rectangular wall, and board-and-batten, which is the wrong detail — the house is T1-11, and a batten stands proud where a groove is cut in.
wingElevation._noteDerived: Nothing here is placed by coordinate. The bays come from the rooms behind the wall; the wall top comes from the massing group's storeys and pitch, so the trim cannot drift off the roof it follows; the belt is crawl + one storey; and the siding's head dies into the frieze and rakes with it. Only the trim's sections and the groove spacing are authored.

entablature._note: The wall top RAKES 1 in 12 — 0.91 ft over 10.9 ft, high toward the primary — and the wing had NO eave trim at all: the roof slab met the stucco with no overhang on this face, no fascia, no shadow line. Bare, a 5 degree slope reads as a roof that has slipped rather than sloped. The frieze and cornice rake with it; the corbels under them stand VERTICAL, and that contrast is what makes the slope read as deliberate. The corbels are the porch's WOOD where the bands are white: a corbel is small and this wall never sees direct sun, so a white one casts nothing and vanishes against a white frieze. Its geometry is taken from the massing group's own storeys and pitch, never authored here, so the trim cannot drift off the roof it follows.

cladding._note: T1-11 — GROOVED plywood siding, not board-and-batten. The distinction is not a naming quibble: a batten stands proud and a groove is cut in, so one is modelled by adding material and the other by leaving a gap. The face is built as strips with the gaps between them over a darker backer that shows through, because a groove reads by its SHADOW and this north wall has none: the dark backer IS the shadow. Fourth time on this elevation that relief has read as nothing and only tone has read at all, after the corbels, the oculus and the battens this replaced.
cladding._noteBelt: The belt is the band's base and its drip, so it projects further than the siding it carries. It runs the FULL wall and turns the east corner like the cornice — a band that dies on a corner reads as a flat pasted on the front. Its top is derived from crawl + storyHeight, never authored.
cladding._noteGrooves: grooveOcFt is a MAXIMUM each run divides evenly, not a pitch, so the grooves stay even whatever the wall works out to. 8 in is standard T1-11 (4 in is the other). The outermost strips run flush into the corner boards: a groove hard against a corner board is a gap, not a groove.

frontage._note: Corner lot: city frontage on the NORTH and WEST lines. The lot itself is flat; the right-of-way falls away from it. The property stands nwDropIn above the sidewalk at the NW corner. Going EAST along the north line that drop dies to zero northLevelFromEastFt short of the NE corner; going SOUTH along the west line it eases to swDropIn at the SW corner. Both work out to a steady ~4% walk.
frontage._noteBandOrder: The two frontages run the same bands in OPPOSITE order — north is (property line) park strip, sidewalk, curb, with the walk out against the asphalt; west is (property line) sidewalk, park strip, curb. Each is sidewalkWidthFt + parkStripWidthFt overall either way, so the curb lines and the paved NW corner block agree.
frontage._noteYard: northYardFt is the CLEAR front yard: outer face of the north exterior wall to the near face of the retaining wall. It sets the north property line, and with it the parcel depth.
frontage._noteEntry: Front entry: a walk crosses the planting strip on the front door's centreline, then entryStepCount steps climb through a gap left in the retaining wall and land at the foot of the porch cascade. The wall is exactly 18 in high at the front door, so three 6 in risers come out even.
